title: Fair Recruitment and Selection Through Relevant Evidence
audience: Supervisor focus; useful for all staff serving on hiring panels or reviewing opportunities.

sources.title: One DSD: Reducing bias in hiring and selection

filename: courses/One DSD - I17 - Fair Recruitment and Selection Through Relevant Evidence.pptx

slides.text:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Fair Recruitment and Selection Through Relevant Evidence
Compare recruitment and selection practices through the capabilities the work actually requires.
Intermediate self-directed learning
slides.narration: Recruitment begins before an interview, when the work is described and the opportunity is made visible. Selection then depends on what evidence is sought and how it is compared. This course examines hiring and service participation decisions, with attention to access, relevant criteria, and consistent reasoning. You will distinguish a genuine capability from familiarity or presentation style. The exercises prepare judgment; they do not approve a hiring method or replace the agency's recruitment, accommodation, or employment processes.

slides.text:
What does 'a good fit' establish?
Privately consider a panel note: 'This candidate felt like a good fit.' What evidence about the work is missing?

A favorable impression may invite examination, but it cannot replace a relevant criterion. Start with the capability the position needs and the evidence that would demonstrate it.
slides.narration: The phrase can hide several different judgments. One panel member may mean analytical skill, another may mean familiar experience, and another may mean an easy conversation. Without examining those meanings, a group can agree while comparing different things. Ask what the person actually demonstrated for the role. The point is not to forbid human impressions; it is to prevent them from becoming an unexplained standard that some applicants can satisfy through resemblance rather than relevant capability.

slides.text:
Capability, criterion, and evidence
A capability is something the work requires. A criterion explains how it will be assessed. Evidence is what the applicant actually demonstrates.

Keep the links visible through the approved process. An impressive title, familiar background, or confident delivery does not automatically establish the capability.
slides.narration: A clear chain improves the comparison. If the role requires reasoning with incomplete information, the question should allow an applicant to show that reasoning. The evidence may include how they identify a gap and compare alternatives. It need not come from the panel's exact workplace unless the real requirement makes that experience necessary. Actual criteria and methods need the appropriate approval. This course offers reasoning examples rather than a replacement rating system or a decision about any real applicant.

slides.text:
Local knowledge without a formal title
In this example, a service advisory opportunity seeks knowledge of access barriers but recognizes only formal job titles. Relevant experience may be excluded.

Compare the stated purpose with the evidence allowed. Repeated title-based gates could narrow whose knowledge informs services; actual rules and effects need examination.
slides.narration: Here staff want useful knowledge, yet the invitation recognizes a narrower form of evidence. Someone who understands a service route through lived or practical experience may not hold the title listed. That does not mean all qualifications should be removed. It means the relationship between the qualification and the purpose should be checked. A revised invitation could make relevant evidence more visible through the appropriate process. Its reach and effects would still need examination before a broader conclusion about inequity.

slides.text:
Knowledge behind a formal title
In this example, a service panel seeks knowledge of access barriers but its invitation recognizes only formal job titles. What should be examined?
A. Whether the title is relevant and what appropriate evidence could demonstrate the needed knowledge.
B. Whether participants can obtain a title before speaking.
C. Whether the same narrow requirement was applied consistently.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: In this example, a service advisory opportunity needs people who understand barriers in the response process. Its invitation lists formal job titles but does not explain why those titles are necessary. Someone with relevant practical knowledge is outside that list. Consider what a fair inquiry should examine before any change is proposed. The exercise does not approve a new participation rule. It asks whether the criterion connects to the purpose and what evidence could demonstrate the capability. A repeated gate might narrow whose knowledge is heard, but the actual effect remains to be established.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Whether the title is relevant and what appropriate evidence could demonstrate the needed knowledge.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Whether participants can obtain a title before speaking.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Whether the same narrow requirement was applied consistently.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
Connect the criterion to the purpose and seek appropriate review. Relevant experience may take more than one form.

What capability does the criterion actually establish?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: The stronger response examines the relationship between the condition and the purpose. A title may be relevant in some circumstances, but it should not substitute automatically for evidence of knowledge. Seek review through the responsible process rather than invent authority to change it. A revised invitation should be examined for actual reach and contribution before claiming it removes a systemic barrier.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
This preserves the gate without examining whether it establishes the needed knowledge.

What capability does the criterion actually establish?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Asking people to obtain a title shifts the burden without clarifying why the title is needed. Practical service knowledge might be relevant even where the person lacks that formal role. The question is not whether every condition should disappear, but whether this condition demonstrates the capability sought. Repeated unnecessary gates could narrow whose experience informs services.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Consistency matters but does not establish relevance. An unnecessary criterion may repeatedly exclude useful expertise.

What capability does the criterion actually establish?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A rule can be consistently applied and still be poorly matched to its purpose. Equal use of the condition does not answer whether it recognizes relevant capability. Examine the work and the evidence the criterion allows, then use the appropriate review route. If changes occur, assess what participation they actually enable rather than assume that a different rule guarantees representation.

slides.text:
Describe the work before the ideal person
Identify necessary results and conditions. Distinguish actual requirements from preferences that resemble the current team.

A familiar background may be useful but should not become an unexplained gate. Questions about approved qualifications and posting language belong with the responsible hiring process.
slides.narration: An idealized picture of the person can import assumptions before staff examine the job. The current team's experience may reflect one successful route, not every route to capability. Describe the actual work, then ask what evidence is necessary. Some conditions may be essential and cannot be changed through a learning activity. Others may be preferences that need review. The useful inquiry connects each criterion to a reason rather than presenting a personal model of professionalism as a requirement everyone must meet.

slides.text:
Make the opportunity understandable
A clear posting explains the work and how the actual application route operates. Outreach also affects who learns about the opportunity.

Use approved channels and accurate information. A publicly available posting does not establish that every relevant applicant encountered or could use it.
slides.narration: Visibility involves more than placing information somewhere public. People need to recognize the opportunity, understand what evidence is sought, and use the application route. Established networks may help some applicants find that information sooner. Community engagement and briefs can prepare questions about reach without assigning recruitment duties by identity. The agency's actual processes guide outreach and posting. Review what the route made possible rather than assume that availability alone demonstrates an equally useful opportunity for everyone.

slides.text:
Ask a question that reveals reasoning
A question about a relevant example can reveal actions, judgment, and results. A vague request to describe fit may reveal mainly self-presentation.

Use the approved question and comparison approach. The prompt should not require private identity experiences or a story from the panel's own workplace unless the requirement establishes that need.
slides.narration: An applicant should have a meaningful way to demonstrate the capability being assessed. In this example, a question might ask how they compared options when information was incomplete. The panel then looks for relevant reasoning rather than a polished performance alone. A person may draw on another work setting or an appropriate hypothetical example. Actual interview design belongs within the hiring process. The course asks you to examine whether the method reveals the intended capability instead of rewarding a narrow style of answering.

slides.text:
Access that preserves the assessed capability
A change in format or an approved support arrangement may allow the same relevant skill to be demonstrated.

Use the proper process for access and accommodations. Identical conditions are not automatically fair when they add an unrelated barrier, and a course cannot approve an exception.
slides.narration: Consistency concerns the relevant assessment and the authorized procedure. It does not require assuming that every detail of the arrangement must be identical regardless of access needs. The appropriate process determines what can change and how the capability remains assessable. Keep medical or other private information within the correct route. A panel should not improvise a favorable arrangement for one candidate or a penalty for another. Clear preparation helps staff respond to interruptions and support questions without changing the standard through personal preference.

slides.text:
When the standard moves after an answer
A panel likes a familiar applicant and begins valuing confidence over the approved evidence of analytical reasoning.

Return to the established criterion and the actual answer. Repeated moving standards can advantage familiarity, even if every decision is described as professional judgment.
slides.narration: Changing the standard after seeing an applicant creates a different comparison. The panel may remember confidence more vividly than the actual reasoning, especially if a senior member expresses enthusiasm early. Locate the evidence each rating uses and compare it with the approved criterion. A genuine concern can still be considered through the proper process. The aim is a reasoned discussion, not automatic consensus. Whether this pattern explains a wider selection difference requires examination of actual decisions and conditions.

slides.text:
A familiar candidate changes the discussion
A panel shifts from analytical evidence to confidence after liking a familiar applicant. What is the best response?
A. Accept the shift because the panel agrees.
B. Return to the approved criterion and the applicant's actual evidence.
C. Reward familiarity as proof of agency readiness.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: In this example, a hiring panel has an approved criterion for reasoning with incomplete evidence. After an applicant feels familiar and speaks confidently, the discussion starts rewarding confidence instead. The panel appears to agree, but its notes do not explain what changed. Consider the distinction between human impressions and the evidence the role requires. The strongest response returns to the actual answer and authorized comparison method. A recurring shift could affect selection opportunity, but this one scene does not establish why a wider disparity exists or what the final hiring result should be.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Accept the shift because the panel agrees.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Return to the approved criterion and the applicant's actual evidence.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Reward familiarity as proof of agency readiness.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Agreement may conceal a changed standard. Locate the evidence rather than treat consensus as justification.

Did the criterion change after the panel saw the person?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Panel agreement does not make a new standard relevant or approved. A confident answer may be memorable while failing to demonstrate the analytical capability being assessed. Examine what each reviewer credited and compare it with the established criterion. Repeated shifts toward favored presentation or familiarity could affect opportunity, but the broader mechanism needs evidence from actual processes.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
The response preserves a reasoned comparison through the approved process. Discuss gaps and disagreements with evidence.

Did the criterion change after the panel saw the person?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: Returning to the approved criterion makes the reasoning inspectable. Ask which part of the answer demonstrates the capability and what remains uncertain. Differences in ratings can then be discussed through notes rather than status or personal enthusiasm. The process should follow its authorized method, with concerns handled appropriately. This does not demand automatic agreement or guarantee a particular selection result.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Familiarity may provide context, but it does not automatically demonstrate the required capability.

Did the criterion change after the panel saw the person?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: An applicant's familiarity may concern some relevant experience, but the panel still needs evidence of the work capability. Treating it as automatic readiness can favor insiders and hide gaps in the answer. Distinguish necessary knowledge from resemblance to current staff. Keep the comparison within approved criteria rather than turn a comfortable conversation into an unspoken selection advantage.

slides.text:
Concrete standards and room for different routes
A rating description should identify relevant evidence rather than a vague impression. It should not demand the panel's exact biography.

An applicant may demonstrate the same capability through another setting. Keep actual anchors and review methods within the approved process.
slides.narration: A scale with numbers can appear precise while hiding different interpretations. One reviewer may credit a described action, while another credits enthusiasm. Concrete evidence descriptions help clarify the difference. At the same time, an example should not be so narrow that only insiders can satisfy it. In the fiction, recognizing uncertainty and explaining a comparison are relevant actions. Actual rating standards need authorization and alignment with the role. This course helps examine the reasoning without supplying a universal scoring rule.

slides.text:
Clarification without coaching a favored answer
A question can clarify what the applicant did. A leading prompt can supply the reasoning the panel hoped to hear.

Use approved probing practices consistently. Familiarity should not determine who receives extra help or which gaps in an answer are overlooked.
slides.narration: Clarification is useful when it reveals evidence rather than creates it. Asking someone to explain their own contribution differs from suggesting the ideal response. If a favored candidate receives more guiding prompts, the opportunity may change in a way the final rating hides. Follow the authorized method for questions and probes. A process concern should be handled through the appropriate route rather than improvised after the fact. Examine what the answer actually establishes and where evidence remains incomplete.

slides.text:
Deliberation grounded in notes
Start with the approved criteria and relevant evidence. A strong first opinion can shape what others remember.

When ratings differ, examine the source of the difference. Do not treat seniority, agreement, or a confident statement as a substitute for the actual answer.
slides.narration: A panel can disagree productively if the conversation returns to evidence. One member may have understood a result as the applicant's own work, while another saw only a team claim. That difference can be examined. The panel should not erase uncertainty merely to finish smoothly or accept a senior member's preference without reasons. Actual procedures guide deliberation and documentation. The useful habit is to make the link between the criterion, the answer, and the conclusion visible enough to inspect.

slides.text:
Community knowledge and relevant expertise
Community experience can deepen understanding of the work and the opportunity. It does not require any panelist or applicant to represent a whole group.

Use briefs to prepare questions about reach and assumptions. Assess the expertise actually needed through appropriate criteria rather than infer it from identity.
slides.narration: Staff can learn from community relationships without turning identity into a qualification or a duty. A panelist may bring valuable knowledge of service communication because of their work and experience, not because they are expected to supply a racial or cultural viewpoint. Applicants also should not have to disclose private experiences to demonstrate capability. Background resources can help staff examine narrow assumptions about relevant experience. Keep the actual task, authorized criteria, and individual evidence at the center of the comparison.

slides.text:
Relevant knowledge and a restricted invitation
A community participant has practical service knowledge but lacks the formal title on an invitation. Staff propose changing nothing because the list is consistent.

Examine what the criterion is for and what evidence could meet the purpose. Consistency does not answer whether the gate is relevant.
slides.narration: Applying the same irrelevant condition to everyone can still narrow useful participation. The fiction asks staff to distinguish a consistent rule from a justified criterion. If the purpose is knowledge of access barriers, examine whether the title actually establishes that knowledge and whether another form of evidence could be appropriate. Do not assume authority to revise the real process. Prepare the question for the responsible role, and assess any revised invitation for what it makes possible and what remains unknown.

slides.text:
A panel member's community role
A panel member is asked to give the view of an entire community because of their identity. What is the more appropriate approach?
A. Make that representative role part of every question.
B. Exclude community knowledge from deliberation.
C. Invite the member's actual expertise without assuming representation.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: In this example, a hiring panel includes a colleague with relevant service expertise. Other members ask the colleague to supply the view of a whole community because of their identity. The colleague's actual knowledge may be useful, but the request presumes a representative duty. Consider how the panel can learn from experience without making one person speak for everyone. The choice should preserve the authorized role, relevant criteria, and individual expertise. Repeated assumptions of this kind could affect whose contributions are recognized and how the work is distributed.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Make that representative role part of every question.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Exclude community knowledge from deliberation.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Invite the member's actual expertise without assuming representation.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Identity does not establish a duty or ability to speak for everyone. The request can restrict the person's professional contribution.

Is expertise being recognized, or a representative duty being assigned?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A panel member can contribute knowledge and experience without holding every view in a community. Assigning that role through identity may place extra explanatory work on them and narrow how colleagues hear their expertise. Ask about the actual contribution relevant to the hiring task. Repeated identity-based roles can affect workload and influence, so examine the arrangement rather than assume inclusion from appearance.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Relevant community knowledge can help examine the work. The concern is presumed representation, not learning from experience.

Is expertise being recognized, or a representative duty being assigned?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Removing all community knowledge would discard relevant learning about service needs and assumptions. The better distinction is between situated expertise and an automatic representative role. A member may know particular work or relationships and can describe the limits of that knowledge. Use it alongside the approved criteria and applicant evidence, without treating one person's account as a whole community answer.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
Recognize individual expertise and the panel's actual responsibilities. Use appropriate sources and criteria for the comparison.

Is expertise being recognized, or a representative duty being assigned?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: This approach allows useful expertise while respecting the member as an individual professional. Clarify their actual panel role and invite relevant perspectives, not an identity-based verdict for everyone. Culture briefs can prepare questions and community relationships can deepen understanding, but neither replaces the authorized selection criteria. A reasoned comparison should remain grounded in what applicants demonstrated for the work.

slides.text:
The repeated route into opportunity
Outreach, criteria, access, probing, and deliberation can interact across many selections.

Trace how a routine changes who can demonstrate capability or whose evidence counts. A selection difference alone cannot establish the cause, but it can prompt a more careful process inquiry.
slides.narration: The systemic mechanism may involve several linked steps rather than one overt statement. A narrow posting could limit who applies, a style-based question could obscure relevant knowledge, and moving standards could favor familiarity. Each link needs evidence. Other requirements and conditions may explain part of the pattern. A review should distinguish the applicant pool, the assessment opportunity, and the result. This supports learning from the process without assuming that every difference proves discrimination or every formal procedure guarantees fairness.

slides.text:
Evidence before a broad finding
Compare the approved standard, the task offered, the actual notes, and the decision process. Record missing information.

Later employee success does not by itself establish that the selection route was fair. Process quality and later performance answer different questions.
slides.narration: A successful hire can coexist with an assessment weakness. Likewise, a disappointing later outcome does not automatically prove a biased selection. Examine whether the questions revealed the intended capabilities and whether ratings used the approved evidence. Relevant records and appropriate review can help identify uncertainty. Keep information permissions and confidentiality in view. The aim is a supportable account of the route, not a retrospective story that treats whichever outcome occurred as proof that the earlier process was either sound or unfair.

slides.text:
Rewrite an impression as an evidence question
Privately revise: 'The candidate is polished and fits our culture.'

Name the actual capability, the evidence needed, and what the supplied answer does or does not establish. Avoid inventing a criterion or replacing a real hiring procedure.
slides.narration: This reflection can use a position requiring clear explanation of a policy question. Ask what clarity means for that task and what the answer demonstrated. Did the applicant explain the condition accurately and identify uncertainty, or did the panel mainly notice style? Keep any relevant communication requirement while removing unexplained impressions. The exercise prepares a better question about evidence. It does not authorize a new rating method or a conclusion about a real candidate's identity, capability, or selection result.

slides.text:
A fair start and later opportunity
Selection influences who enters the workforce; onboarding and development influence whether the demonstrated capability can grow.

Carry clear expectations and workable access into later stages. Examine whether opportunities and feedback remain connected to the work rather than a continuing judgment of fit.
slides.narration: Recruitment is one part of the employee life cycle, not its conclusion. A new colleague may need local process knowledge and support to use the capability they demonstrated. Development assignments and feedback can then either extend opportunity or repeat familiar preferences. Connect each stage to actual work and evidence. Community-informed service learning can deepen knowledge without making employees representatives by identity. A stronger process remains open to reviewing both the entry route and the conditions that follow.

slides.text:
Compare for the work, through the proper process
Use relevant capabilities, clear criteria, workable access, and consistent evidence. Keep authority and privacy within the actual hiring route.

When a repeated practice narrows opportunity, examine its mechanism and effects. A fair account preserves uncertainty instead of substituting familiarity or outcomes for evidence.
slides.narration: The course's central distinction is between recognizing the work and recognizing someone who feels familiar. Clear criteria and appropriate procedures help staff examine relevant knowledge while preserving access and responsibilities. Human judgment remains necessary, but its reasons should be understandable. Continue asking what the evidence demonstrates, what is missing, and whether the assessment route adds an unrelated barrier. That approach can support recruitment and later opportunity without replacing the agency's employment processes or claiming a cause that has not been established.

outcomes: Distinguish necessary job capabilities from familiar credentials or preferences.
Examine who can find and use the opportunity.
Compare candidates using stable criteria and relevant evidence.
Identify a possible selection barrier without treating a training activity as an authorized employment decision.
